## Summary
A seven-step maturity ladder for companies going from AI tool adoption to an agentic org. The diagnostic punchline: **most companies sit on step one while shopping for step-seven technology — what they actually lack is step-four discipline.**

1. **Tool adoption** — AI tools exist across the org, a human runs each one. Developer closes the lid, automations die; somebody goes on vacation, the workflow goes with them.
2. **Context layer** — knowledge graphs per department, each behind its own API gateway. Sales queries engineering through an API. Separated domains keep agents from hallucinating across departmental boundaries.
3. **Harness engineering** — build evals, routing logic, and quality gates *before* picking a model; the LLM comes in last. "Your harness is your IP and your capex. The model underneath is a commodity you swap when something better ships. If changing the LLM breaks your system, you built a dependency, not a platform."
4. **Go headless** — host every automation outside a laptop; it fires on schedule, on conditions, without a human logging in at 9am. Companies stall here because nobody forces the migration from "script on my desktop" to "service that runs on its own."
5. **Governance** — RBAC on every knowledge structure from day one. TTL on every agent: "Dead agents are tech debt with active API keys." Past 100 tools you need lifecycle management — retire anything idle 90 days, deprecate anything whose eval scores drop below threshold.
6. **Agent-to-agent** — stitch headless instances into a value chain; Agent A finishes, hands off to Agent B, with an LLM sitting between them as a quality gate judging every handoff.
7. **Step functions** — orchestrated, semi/fully automated workflows. Agents handle volume, humans handle exceptions; the org runs on agent output.

Closing anecdote: they walked a VP of Engineering through all seven — "You're on step one. But over a hundred tools means step four is closer than you think."

## Why it matters
- **The ladder is descriptive, not prescriptive — and that's the test it invites.** Its real value is as a *self-audit*: the user's Paperclip companies can be scored against it honestly. The relay that carried this very tweet is the counter-example to step one: this capture ran headless (step 4), woke on traffic (event-conditioned, not 9am-login), with scoped keys per channel (step 5's RBAC instinct) and a non-LLM daemon as the deterministic base layer. The gap areas are the honest ones: no per-department context graph with API gateways (step 2 is partly satisfied by profile isolation, not by design), and eval scores don't yet drive agent retirement (step 5's deprecation rule is a policy this org has never written down).
- **Step 3 is the "harness is the IP" argument, stated at org scale** — direct match to [[2026-09-14-rauchg-verifiers-skills-new-frameworks]]: verifiers and skills (not model choice) are the durable asset, because the model layer commoditizes. Ajzenstadt adds the swap test as the failure detector: if changing the LLM breaks the system, you built a dependency, not a platform.
- **Step 5's "dead agents are tech debt with active API keys" is the sharpest line in the piece** — TTL and the 90-day/eval-threshold retirement rules are concrete and checkable. The org-design cousin of [[2026-10-18-copyconstruct-claude-md-curated-corpus]]: curation of what agents may know (context hygiene) pairs with lifecycle discipline over what agents may do.
- **Steps 4→6 are this vault's running theme, formalized.** Step 4 (headless) = [[2026-10-10-diegohaz-background-agents-not-subagents]] — background agents as the attention-preserving primitive; step 6's LLM-judged handoffs need exactly the observability of [[2026-10-19-flohoeller-agent-tree-component]]; step 7's step-function workflows = [[2026-10-24-kunchen-attention-bottleneck-step-functions]], where each orchestration change showed up as a visible step up in PR velocity. Ajzenstadt's ladder is the org chart of what those notes showed in one dev's ledger.
- **The endpoint rhymes with Calvin's bottleneck thesis.** "Agents handle volume, humans handle exceptions" is [[2026-10-24-calvingrunewald-minimize-human-attention]] stated as an org-design target — the whole ladder is a sequence of attention buybacks.
- **Skepticism gates:** it's a maturity model, and maturity models sell consulting — the seven steps are unfalsiable as stated (any org can be placed anywhere, and "you need step-four discipline" is always available advice); no company is named as having climbed past step four, and the VP-of-Engagement anecdote is a sales vignette; "knowledge graph per department behind an API gateway" is a big architectural claim asserted in one sentence with no failure modes; the step-5 thresholds (100 tools, 90 days, eval-threshold) are stated as universals but are almost certainly context-dependent; and the ladder implies strict sequencing, while real orgs commonly run steps 4 and 5 concurrently with step 2 retrofits. Useful as a checklist, not as a law.
